posts.title: The Tamagotchification of AI
posts.description: Other people’s AI outputs often feel strangely hollow. Silicon Valley has figured out how to bind us to our increasingly personal chatbots, digital “pets” we are meant to keep feeding with our data.

posts.title: The Politics of Sociological “Liquidation”
posts.description: Those who would see sociology unmade are aligned, consciously or not, with a powerful reactionary force working to remold the academy—and the world.

posts.title: Elon Musk for the Not-So-Perplexed
posts.description: Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff’s “Muskism” is a much-needed critical study of the world’s first trillionaire. But Musk is no enigma—and no mere symptom either.

posts.title: One Giant Leap for Oligarchy
posts.description: When a trillionaire controls essential infrastructure, democracy suffers.

posts.title: AI and the Means of Intellectual Production
posts.description: AI isn’t so much a break with past history as a continuation of capitalism’s accelerating tendencies—with humanity’s collective data as its training set, and with millions of jobs at risk.

posts.title: Have Denmark’s Right-Leaning Social Democrats Finally Learned Their Lesson?
posts.description: Denmark’s recent elections suggest the Social Democrats’ rightward turn on immigration won’t always win. Voters expect more from the left—even in the age of Trump, Meloni, and Farage.

posts.title: The Trillion-Dollar Vassal
posts.description: How Trump 2.0, Israel’s Gaza war, and Norway's two-trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund converged in a firestorm of finance, geopolitics, and genocide.

posts.title: Dan Wang's "Breakneck": A Lesson in Disavowed Hawkishness
posts.description: Like Klein and Thompson's Abundance, Dan Wang wants the U.S. to build. But Breakneck isn't about raising living standards—it's about preparing for war.

posts.title: Picaresque Postmodernism in Dangerous Times
posts.description: Why Paul Thomas Anderson's "One Battle After Another" doesn't work in this political moment.

posts.title: Harris’s 107 Days and the Missing Reckoning: Gaza
posts.description: Early coverage of Kamala Harris’s campaign memoir, 107 Days, has been unfair. Yet Harris still won't adequately deal with the Biden administration's complicity in the Gaza genocide, or her own role.

posts.title: The Poverty of Abundance
posts.description: Abundance liberalism won't defeat fascism.

posts.title: Norway's Right is Obsessed With Immigration and Crime
posts.description: Norway is a safe, prosperous, and diverse society. So why can't the right stop talking about immigration and crime?

posts.title: Lemkin's Concept of Genocide
posts.description: A 1945 letter from jurist Raphael Lemkin takes us back to a historical moment when the concept of genocide was just beginning to take hold.

posts.title: Ringo's "Peace and Love" and the Problem of the Empty Signifier
posts.description: Ringo Starr just wants "peace and love." What could possibly be wrong with that?

posts.title: Review: Not Enough Fight
posts.description: 'Fight' by Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes offers a gripping account of the 2024 presidential election, placing blame on both Biden and Harris for Trump's victory.

posts.title: The Dangers of TACO
posts.description: Trump Always Chickens Out, or TACO, was a playful way of criticizing Trump's early second-term policies. But goading Trump into taking a firmer stance is a risky move.

posts.title: Shock and Subordination: The First 100 Days of Trump 2.0
posts.description: Trump's desire for power seems limitless. But people are beginning to wake up to the real-world consequences of his policies.

posts.title: Trump’s Nordic Encounter
posts.description: The Global South knows what US imperialism means. The Nordic countries are beginning to catch on.

posts.title: Between MAGA and a Hard Place
posts.description: Two books—one on Steve Bannon and the global far right, the other on life at a Chinese university—reveal a world increasingly riven by competing ideologies.

posts.title: The Great American Decoupling
posts.description: Under Trump 2.0, the U.S. is decoupling from the world—and the world from it. Both are worse off for it.

posts.title: What’s the Matter with Kentucky?
posts.description: Are Trumpists found—or made? A ground-level report from eastern Kentucky only tells half the story.

posts.title: The AI Hype Bubble
posts.description: And its cognitive, social, and financial risks.

posts.title: The Courts and the Street
posts.description: Judges can serve as critical bulwarks against an authoritarian turn. But in the end, only grassroots organizing and a mass popular movement can truly withstand authoritarianism.

posts.title: Technofeudalism and Telecoms
posts.description: Taking a closer look at two books—Yanis Varoufakis's 'Technofeudalism' and Eva Dou's 'House of Huawei'—reveals the deep entanglement of technology and politics.

posts.title: The Specter of Inflation
posts.description: The far right has weaponized inflation. We should critically examine how nationalist movements activate and manipulate ideas about economic hardship for political gain.

posts.title: Fluid Fascism
posts.description: Combining the concept of diagonalism with Zygmunt Bauman's "liquid modernity" allows us to better grasp Trump's flexible ideology.

posts.title: The Blitzkrieg President
posts.description: Trump's first weeks back in power have aimed to disorient and demoralize—and so, to begin the work of dismantling liberal democracy.

posts.title: The New Fascist International
posts.description: A growing club of far-right, hardline nationalist, and fascist political leaders is working hard to transform the world. They must be opposed.

posts.title: Highlight the Contradictions!
posts.description: Trump's coalition is filled with contradictions that threaten its stability. The Left should highlight these weaknesses while advancing a bold vision of its own.

posts.title: A Streetcar Named Greenland
posts.description: Trump wants to wrest control of Greenland from Denmark. But replacing a former colonizer with a global hegemon is only a recipe for deeper subjugation, not freedom.

posts.title: 2024 in Review: A Year of Political Reaction
posts.description: If we want a better world in 2025, we need to start by reading and thinking our way out of the growing global polycrisis.

posts.title: Proust's Housekeeper
posts.description: Céleste Albaret invites us to share in the delight that a person like Marcel Proust, for all his strangeness, ever walked among us.

posts.title: In Praise of Planning
posts.description: In our crisis-ridden world, could centralized economic planning, rather than the ideal of free markets, be the solution?

posts.title: The Reagan Dream
posts.description: Despite his admiration, Trump is no Reagan: While conservatives aim to conserve, extremists want to push against all limits, venturing into the great beyond—a potentially abyssal, violent beyond.

posts.title: How to Buy Power and Influence People
posts.description: Musk's Twitter takeover makes little business sense, but it has given the world's richest man a global megaphone and easy access to Trump's incoming second White House.

posts.title: Fascism vs. Centrism
posts.description: The stakes have seldom been higher. Enabling the rise of neofascism would be a historic mistake for the left.

posts.title: Trump as Apprentice—or Master?
posts.description: A recent biopic, The Apprentice (2024), prioritizes aesthetics over substance, downplaying Trump’s personal responsibility for his profound character flaws.

posts.title: The Madness of Civil War
posts.description: Returning to Alex Garland's 'Civil War' (2024) leaves a mixed impression, but its core theme is, unfortunately, more relevant than ever.

posts.title: Critique and Conspiracy
posts.description: How can we distinguish between problematic or dangerous conspiracy theories and legitimate intellectual critique?

posts.title: Stuart Hall, An Intellectual for Times of Reaction
posts.description: In troubling times, we should return to Stuart Hall, a remarkable political thinker and cultural analyst.

posts.title: An Eyeless Gaze on Gaza
posts.description: We know the facts about the war on Gaza. But facts alone don't make for actionable truth.

posts.title: Ethnonationalist Bloat, or Where Does a Country’s “Feeling of Fullness” Come From?
posts.description: Anti-immigration movements often speak of their country being full. But with the right policies, there's plenty of room for everyone.

posts.title: Ontocide: The Despair of Gaza
posts.description: Ontocide destroys the will to care about things in the world. Together with politicide and genocide, it forms the “dark triad of occupation”: destroy the state, the people, and meaning as such.

posts.title: The Nexus of the Presidency
posts.description: Overemphasizing Biden’s verbal gaffes risks falling prey to a reactionary politics of the performance: What matters more is the nexus of forces the President surrounds himself with.

posts.title: The Upside-Down Philosopher
posts.description: Reviewing Slavoj Žižek's 'Freedom: A Disease Without a Cure' (2023).

posts.title: Artificial Unintelligence (AU) and the Problem of Perpetual Patchability
posts.description: AI systems are fundamentally dumb, but they're always being improved -- or so their makers say. How to critique an object that is forever being unmade and remade?

posts.title: Social Democracy, or Defending the National Interest
posts.description: Truly attending to the world’s problems would mean abandoning the parochial, nation-centered vision of social democracy for something like a true internationalism.

posts.title: Post-Politics and Technocracy: Taking "People Power" Seriously Again
posts.description: Defeating the rising far right also means combating the post-political ideal of technocratic governance.

posts.title: Unpacking Stalin's Library
posts.description: The puzzle of a murderous dictator who was also a voracious reader remains unsolved despite the author's efforts.

posts.title: The Gourmand as Class Warrior
posts.description: Dwight Garner (2023), "The Upstairs Delicatessen: On Eating, Reading, Reading About Eating, and Eating While Reading." New York: Farrar, Strauss and Giroux.

posts.title: Israel/Gaza: The Economic Consequences of War, the Economic Prospects for Peace
posts.description: Wars are costly—so can Israel afford not to turn a truce into a more lasting peace?

posts.title: Jean-Pierre Dupuy (2023), ‘The War That Must Not Occur’
posts.description: Nuclear deterrence works—until it doesn’t. A philosopher explores the narrow margin between necessity and catastrophe.

posts.title: Flattening Gaza: Israel's Politics of Destruction and the Problem of the "Arab Body"
posts.description: Israel is pursuing a destructive politics of dispersal-and-flattening in Gaza. But the conception of the "Arab body" that underpins it is hardly new.

posts.title: Shadi Bartsch (2023), ‘Plato Goes to China: The Greek Classics and Chinese Nationalism’
posts.description: What happens when the Greek classics travel to Xi's China and are appropriated to promote "hexie," or harmony?

posts.title: Wall Street, Silicon Valley, and the Vanishing Worker: The Trouble with Joseph Vogl’s “Capital and Ressentiment”
posts.description: Is our era really defined by financialized information capitalism—or are we mistaking the surface for the structure? Amid the new, much of the old still remains.

posts.title: Lionel Barber (2021), 'The Powerful and the Damned: Private Diaries in Turbulent Times'
posts.description: The rich and powerful know all too well the power of the press and will do a great deal to keep it in a state of obeisance.

posts.title: Sociodicy (Key Concept)
posts.description: Examining an under-utilized concept, invoked by the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu.

posts.title: Nixon's Madman Theory
posts.description: Taking a closer look at Nixon's presidency and his so-called madman theory of foreign policy.
